ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Follicle‑stimulating hormone (FSH) is a pituitary gonadotropin that drives gametogenesis and follicle development. It works with LH and feedback hormones to regulate fertility in both sexes.

sections.p: FSH is a glycoprotein hormone secreted by anterior pituitary gonadotrophs. It circulates to the gonads where it binds specific receptors on Sertoli cells (male) and granulosa cells (female).
b: Molecular weight ~30 kDa, two subunits (α shared, β unique).
Peak mid‑follicular phase in women; relatively constant low level in men.

sections.p: In males, FSH stimulates Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis and produce inhibin. In females, it promotes granulosa cell proliferation and aromatase activity, converting androgens to estradiol.
b: FSH → G‑protein → cAMP → gene transcription in target cells.
Aromatase up‑regulation is essential for estrogen synthesis.

sections.p: FSH secretion is controlled by GnRH pulses, negative feedback from inhibin (male) and estradiol (female), and to a lesser extent by activin and follistatin.

t.b: Is the gonadotropin axis suppressed, normal, or hyperactive? Low suggests pituitary failure; high suggests primary gonadal failure.
Assesses Sertoli cell function; low in testicular failure.
Helps interpret FSH in menstrual disorders; high estradiol suppresses FSH.

sections.p: Abnormal FSH leads to infertility, gonadal dysgenesis, or premature ovarian failure. Both excess and deficiency have distinct clinical patterns.
b: FSH deficiency – pituitary adenoma, Sheehan syndrome, hypopituitarism.
FSH excess – primary gonadal failure, Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome.

sections.p: Understanding FSH guides evaluation of infertility, delayed puberty, and menstrual irregularities, and informs use of assisted reproductive technologies.
b: Low FSH with low LH → central hypogonadism; treat with pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropins.
High FSH with high LH → primary gonadal failure; focus on hormone replacement.

t.b: Distinguishes pituitary from hypothalamic failure; rise in FSH/LH confirms pituitary reserve.
Identifies chromosomal causes (e.g., Turner, Klinefelter) when FSH is markedly elevated.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams: FSH’s target cells, feedback loops, and how patterns of FSH/LH differentiate central vs. primary gonadal disorders.
b: FSH ↑ in primary ovarian failure; ↓ in hypopituitarism.
Inhibin B is a useful marker of Sertoli cell activity.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute pituitary apoplexy causing sudden loss of FSH/LH with severe headache and visual loss.
Rapid ovarian failure with high FSH and menopausal symptoms in a young woman.

faq.q: Why does FSH rise after menopause?
faq.a: Ovarian follicles are depleted, so inhibin and estradiol fall, removing negative feedback and causing FSH to increase.

faq.q: Can low FSH cause infertility in men?
faq.a: Yes; insufficient stimulation of Sertoli cells reduces spermatogenesis, leading to oligospermia or azoospermia.

faq.q: Is FSH measurement useful in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?
faq.a: FSH is usually normal or low; the LH:FSH ratio >2 is a classic but not diagnostic feature.

exam: Explain how FSH and inhibin interact in the feedback regulation of the menstrual cycle.
Differentiate central from primary hypogonadism using FSH, LH, and inhibin levels.
Describe the role of FSH in spermatogenesis and the consequences of its deficiency.
